newsitem.title: UK: BOXING-I'M BETTER THAN ALI WAS, SAYS FEATHERWEIGHT HAMED.
newsitem.headline: BOXING-I'M BETTER THAN ALI WAS, SAYS FEATHERWEIGHT HAMED.

text.p: World featherweight champion Naseem Hamed, known as Prince Naseem and noted for his leopard-skin shorts, proclaims he is a better boxer than Muhammad Ali was.
Just as Ali did in his heyday, Britain's Hamed is proving he is his own greatest promoter and a contender for the generation's champion of hyperbole.
"It is a big statement to make, that man was legend and hopefully I will be a legend," 22-year-old diminutive Hamed told reporters this week.

Hamed is currently hot on the warpath as he makes final preparations before facing veteran Tom Johnson in a bid to unify his World Boxing Organisation (WBO) title with the American's International Boxing Federation (IBF) belt in the London Arena on Saturday.
Hamed's abundant confidence and cocky antics in the ring have won him large purses and sponsorship deals but earned criticism from pundits who reckon he cannot live up to his own hype.

Saturday's fight will be his biggest to date and he intends to silence the critics who reserve judgement on the big-talking featherweight despite 24 straight wins, 22 inside the distance, and four successful defences of his WBO belt.
Hamed, or "Prince Naseem" as he calls himself, has told the public he intends to knock "Boom boom" Johnson out in the third round -- shades of Ali.
"Sounds good, doesn't it?" Hamed said, chuckling.
"It's America against the Brits and the Arab world, and we ain't losing this one. Full stop," Hamed told reporters. He later dedicated the bout to his mother.
Hamed has a huge following in his parents' native country of Yemen, but he said he was proud to be born and bred in Sheffield, in England's industrial heartland.
"I'm a British Arab," he grinned, lolling in his chair.
Asked about Saturday's fight strategy, Hamed said, "I'm gonna wait... I'm gunning to make my prediction come true. Inshallah, God willing."
Hamed has always thanked Allah for his talents and says his punches are heaven-sent. "I see myself better than Ali. I can do more stuff than Ali," he argued.
His trainer, manager and long-time mentor, Brendan Ingle, said: "He's making moves other fighters can only dream about."

Ingle sees Hamed as in a class of his own, capable of leading with either hand, switch mid-fight, box the English orthodox style favoured by most, stand square-on to his opponent or come at him from the side.
"Muhammad Ali...only boxed orthodox," Ingle said in his thick Irish accent. "He [Hamed] can box five ways and you've got to nail him to the floor to beat him."

Ingle is convinced there has not been a fighter of his calibre for 40 years. "He has balance, timing, co-ordination... even when he has leaped in and missed, the opponent hasn't been able to take advantage of it.," Ingle said.
Hamed's million pound sponsorship deal with sport-shoe maker Adidas shows that his camp are not the only people to think he is a winner. "I'm a very marketable young man," Hamed declared.
Last year, Hamed released a song titled "Walk like a champion, talk like a champion" which became a top 20 hit in the British charts.
He declined comment on how much he stood to make from Saturday's bout, but said: "I'm getting paid a very, very obscene amount of money."

Hamed will be sporting his trademark leopard-skin shorts with "Prince" printed across his waist in large gold letters. "It's different. The leopard is a great animal. It's fast, it's bouncy," he said.
Ali is remembered for floating like a butterfly and stinging like a bee. Asked how his fans would remember him, Hamed said: "Maybe a leopard, but a lot of people say a cobra.
"At the end of the day, I'm Prince, an original fighter. Unique."
